standard.title: Cultural connectedness to place
standard.description: the cultural connectedness of people to places and how this influences their identity, sense of belonging and perceptions of a place, in particular the cultural connectedness of First Nations Australians to Country/Place
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have completed K05 and K06 — they understand liveability as concept, know that cultural factors influence residential decisions, and can analyse implications of service distribution. From K03 they understand multilayered values (including spiritual/cultural) of water for First Nations Australians. This standard extends that understanding to place identity, belonging and inclusion/exclusion more broadly.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how cultural connectedness to places influences identity, belonging and perceptions, especially for First Nations Australians.

nodes.label: Inclusion, exclusion and sense of belonging in places
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify different places where people feel included or excluded and explain how this affects perceptions of liveability.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least one example of a place where a group feels included and one where a group feels excluded, explaining how each affects liveability perception.
nodes.typical_width: Students identify different places where people feel included or excluded, safe or threatened, and explain how these experiences of belonging or exclusion affect perceptions of a place's liveability — recognising that the same physical place can produce different belonging experiences for different groups.
wider: Examine how the built environment signals inclusion or exclusion — e.g. bilingual signage, accessible design, culturally appropriate facilities — and consider what physical changes signal whose belonging matters

Analyse a specific case of a place that has become associated with inclusion for one group and exclusion for another (e.g. a park that young people use for gathering but where elderly residents feel unsafe)
Research how gentrification alters belonging experiences — long-term residents may be economically displaced from places central to their cultural identity
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that belonging is place-specific and group-specific is the foundation for understanding First Nations connectedness to Country/Place in node 2. Without grasping that the same place produces different belonging experiences for different groups, students cannot engage with the specificity and depth of First Nations place relationships.

response_modes.reason: Students tend to treat safety and inclusion as universal — if a place is safe/inclusive for them, it is for everyone. Explicitly scaffolding the perspective-taking required to understand differential belonging experiences is the key teaching move here.

Using multiple examples across age groups, cultural groups and settlement types ensures students understand that inclusion/exclusion in place is a widespread geographical phenomenon, not an edge case.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The inclusion/exclusion analysis applies across all communities — it supports rich local fieldwork (comparing how different groups experience the same local place) and connects to K08 strategies for improving liveability for specific groups.
success_criteria: Identifies at least one example of inclusion and one of exclusion in a specific place, naming the group affected in each case.
Explains how feelings of safety, threat, inclusion or exclusion affect perceptions of a place's liveability.

nodes.label: Social connection and liveability
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the importance of social connectedness and its effect on perceptions of liveability.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain at least two ways that social connectedness affects how people perceive the liveability of a place.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the importance of people being socially connected — through community, cultural groups, family and social networks — and explain how presence or absence of social connection affects perceptions of liveability in different place types.
wider: Examine social isolation in different contexts — elderly people in outer suburbs, young people in remote areas, recently arrived migrants in new cities — and compare how geographic context compounds or alleviates social disconnection
Investigate how digital connectivity has altered social connection in place-based communities and whether virtual social connection substitutes for physical co-presence
Analyse how COVID-19 lockdowns provided a large-scale 'natural experiment' in the liveability effects of reduced social connectivity

response_modes.reason: Examining social connection/disconnection in diverse contexts — remote, urban, elderly, young, newly arrived — prevents students from treating social connectedness as uniform and reveals how place and social context interact.

success_criteria: Explains at least two ways that social connectedness affects perceptions of liveability.
Uses a specific place example to illustrate how social connection or disconnection shapes how a place feels to live in.

nodes.label: First Nations Australians: connectedness and belonging to Country/Place
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can discuss the cultural connectedness and belonging that First Nations Australians have to a range of places through family, Country/Place, dispossession, relocation and employment.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the cultural connectedness and belonging that First Nations Australians have to Country/Place, using at least one dimension (family, Country, dispossession or relocation).
nodes.typical_width: Students discuss the cultural connectedness and belonging that First Nations Australians have to Country/Place through family ties, Country/Place identity, and the ongoing effects of dispossession, relocation and employment on relationships to place — recognising that connections persist across multiple places and are affected but not erased by displacement.
wider: Examine the historical geography of dispossession and relocation for a specific community — trace how policy (missions, reserves, forced removal) altered relationships to Country and the ongoing consequences for place connectedness today
Research how Native Title and land rights frameworks recognise and partly restore First Nations connections to Country — what does legal recognition mean for cultural connectedness?
Examine contemporary First Nations urban identity — how do Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people maintain connection to Country while living far from ancestral lands?
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not grasp the depth and specificity of First Nations connectedness to Country — particularly the way dispossession constitutes a liveability harm beyond physical displacement — will be unable to properly evaluate liveability strategies for First Nations communities in K08.

response_modes.reason: Students may initially understand First Nations connection to Country as analogous to any person's attachment to a home place. The reasoning scaffold needed is to explain how Country relationship is ontological (defines identity and belonging in a fundamental way) rather than merely sentimental — and how dispossession therefore causes a distinctive form of harm.

Examining multiple dimensions of connectedness (family, Country, spiritual, employment) and how dispossession has affected each dimension prevents a one-dimensional understanding of a complex, layered relationship.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The geography of dispossession and its ongoing consequences for place connectedness is one of the most historically and socially significant geographical stories in Australia. Students who engage with multiple dimensions and specific community histories develop richer geographical understanding and better ethical reasoning.
success_criteria: Explains the cultural connectedness and belonging of First Nations Australians to Country/Place, identifying at least two dimensions of that connection.
Explains how dispossession or relocation has affected First Nations relationships to Country, using specific reference to historical or contemporary experience.

nodes.label: Integration: cultural connectedness, identity and liveability perceptions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students explain how cultural connectedness to places influences identity, sense of belonging and perceptions of liveability — integrating inclusion/exclusion analysis, social connection and First Nations Country relationships.
nodes.minimum_width: Students produce an explanation connecting cultural connectedness to either identity, belonging or liveability perception for a specific group.
nodes.typical_width: Students produce an integrated explanation of how cultural connectedness to places shapes identity, belonging and liveability perceptions — applying this to at least two different groups (e.g. First Nations Australians and another cultural group) and explaining how geographical context affects the nature and depth of those connections.
wider: Develop a comparative analysis of cultural connectedness to the same urban place for two different groups — e.g. a long-term Aboriginal urban community and a recently arrived migrant community — examining how their connections are similar and different in nature and liveability implications
Evaluate how a specific liveability strategy (K08) takes cultural connectedness into account — does it strengthen or threaten the place connections of any group?

response_modes.reason: The standard draws together inclusion/exclusion, social connection, and First Nations connectedness into a unified explanation of how cultural belonging shapes place perception. Integration practises making these three threads work together in a coherent argument.

success_criteria: Produces an explanation that connects cultural connectedness to at least two of: identity, belonging, or liveability perception.
Addresses First Nations Australians' connectedness to Country/Place as a specific case within the explanation.
